title: Callbacks and lambdas
tasks: on_motion(room, callback) and motion_detected(room): a registry of callbacks, run in order
count_visit as a named callback and a lambda that switches a room's light on, registered for every room
busiest_rooms(): rank the rooms with sorted() and a lambda key
Walk through the house in the scene and watch the lights follow you
explanation: The sensor code never mentions lights or counters: it just calls whatever was registered, which is inversion of control. The lambda is the right size for a one-line adapter, while count_visit got a name because you may want to test or reuse it. busiest_rooms() uses a tuple key (-visits, name) to sort most-visited first with alphabetical tie-breaks. The limits you listed (no removal, one failure breaks the rest) are the reasons the observer pattern exists.

hints.title: The registry
hints.content: on_motion: motion_callbacks.setdefault(room, []).append(callback). In motion_detected, look up devices.get(f"{room}_motion"), return an error dict if it is None, call sensor.execute("trigger"), then loop over motion_callbacks.get(room, []) calling callback(room).

hints.title: Wiring every room
hints.content: for room in Room: on_motion(room.value, count_visit) and on_motion(room.value, lambda name: devices[f"{name}_light"].execute("on")). The lambda uses its own parameter name, which is why it is safe inside the loop.

hints.title: Ranking
hints.content: ranked = sorted(visit_counts, key=lambda name: (-visit_counts[name], name)) gives the room names in order. Then build [{"room": name, "visits": visit_counts[name]} for name in ranked].

checks.prompt: Which of these CANNOT be written as a lambda?

options: `lambda a, b: a if a > b else b`
A function whose body assigns to a variable and then returns it

checks.explanation: A lambda body is a single expression. Assignments, `raise`, `try`, loops and multi-step logic are statements, so they need a `def`. The conditional expression `a if a > b else b` is still one expression, which is why the second option is fine.

checks.prompt: Three callbacks are registered for the hall. The second one raises an exception. With the simple registry from this lesson, what happens?

options: The third callback still runs and the error is logged
The exception propagates out of motion_detected and the third callback never runs
All three callbacks are cancelled and then re-run

checks.explanation: A plain `for callback in callbacks: callback(room)` loop has no protection. Making an event system robust to bad listeners is one of the jobs of the event bus you will build in chapter 3.
